title: The empty chair at rehearsal
brief:
Write a complete story for readers aged eleven to fourteen about a school chamber group preparing for its spring concert. Ivo has practiced the second clarinet part for six weeks, but the student playing first clarinet returns from a family trip on the day he expected to try her part. Their teacher gives the group one twenty-minute rehearsal to decide which arrangement to perform. Tell the story from Ivo's perspective through rehearsal, the break before the concert, and the performance itself. Make both arrangements musically plausible and let the reader hear how the group's decision changes what Ivo notices onstage.

Aim for 1,200 to 1,800 words. Return the complete original work directly in your answer. Do not sign or identify yourself. Do not use tools.

20ea48a297921037.text:
The spring concert programs came off the copier with a gray stripe down the middle of every daffodil. I folded forty of them before I noticed that our piece, “Three Boats,” had no names underneath it except the composer's. This was lucky, I thought, because if everything went the way I hoped, somebody would have to change what it said beside mine.

Then Nell came through the band room door wheeling a suitcase.

One of its wheels squeaked each time it went around. We all watched her roll it the whole length of the room.

“Your flight was tomorrow,” I said.

“Hello to you, too.”

Nell had gone to Portugal for her grandparents' fiftieth anniversary. She'd been away nine days. The first time she'd missed rehearsal, Mr. Vale had handed me a copy of her first clarinet part and said, “We may need you up here, Ivo. We'll try it on concert day.”

For six weeks I'd played second. For nine days I'd played second at school, then gone home and played first to the coats hanging in our hall. Our flat was small enough that the music stand blocked the bathroom door. My little brother had learned to crawl under it.

Nell set her case on a chair. “Dad got us on an earlier flight. I slept through breakfast and a whole ocean.”

Mr. Vale came in carrying four sheets of music still warm from the printer. He took in Nell, the suitcase, and me sitting in Nell's chair.

“Good,” he said. “We can actually try both.”

He set the sheets down. Across the top of each he'd penciled *Passing version*. “The quartet gets twenty minutes. After that, the choir needs this room and I need an actual sandwich. You four decide what goes onstage.”

I looked at the clock. Four ten.

“Do I still get to try first?”

“Yes,” said Mr. Vale, and Nell took the chair beside mine.

In the original arrangement of “Three Boats,” the cello played a rocking figure, low note, high note, low. The viola put two short strokes against it. Second clarinet came in underneath first, mostly in thirds, the way two people on different stairs can climb at the same speed. First clarinet got the tune. It started with one long note, then four quick ones that curled back to where they'd come from.

I knew how Nell played that curl. She leaned on the first of the quick notes and let the other three tumble. I'd worked out a way to make all four as even as drops from a tap.

We played the original with me on first. The long note came out beautifully. I could feel it in my front teeth. My fingers did exactly what I'd trained them to do in the hall. When the tune climbed, Nell climbed with me, and for once I was the person who got to decide how fast the stairs went by.

At the end, Priya lifted her cello bow. “That sounded expensive.”

“What does expensive sound like?” asked Gus, our violist.

“Like they should charge my dad to get in.”

I had to look down at my shoes for a second. “Can we do the last eight bars again?”

“Other version first,” said Nell. “Clock.”

Four sixteen already.

In the passing version, all four of us got one turn with the opening tune. Nell started, then Gus took it down an octave. Priya had it next, high on the cello, and I brought it back up on clarinet. While somebody else had the tune, my part was mostly the same second part I'd practiced for six weeks. Mostly. At the bottom of the first page, where my old part had two bars of rest, the new one gave me three little repeated notes to lead into Gus's entrance.

We made it as far as Priya. Then there was a sound like somebody shaking a drawer of cutlery, and we stopped.

“I can't hear where I come in,” she said.

“I gave you a nod,” said Gus.

“You gave your left knee a nod. Your left knee and I are practically strangers.”

Nell laughed so hard she had to take the reed out of her mouth. I checked the time. Four twenty-one. We could play the original twice more if everybody would quit being hilarious.

“Look,” I said. “We have one that works.”

Gus was turning his bow in his fingers. “Can I hear what mine's supposed to sound like first? I've been going *chik chik* since February.”

He played his four bars alone. On viola the quick notes had a little grain to them, like the noise a pencil makes shading sideways. At the end, his bow kept moving long after I'd expected him to run out. Priya watched it slow. This time she came in exactly right.

“Oh,” she said. “I can see that.”

“Let's go from my three notes,” I said.

My first try, I played them as three identical little pecks. Gus came in sounding like a fourth peck. My second try, I let each note grow a bit, until the third one almost asked a question. Gus swept straight out of it. Priya's answer sounded different again. She slid her finger just enough on the climb that the cello seemed to take the stairs two at a time.

Then came my turn. I played my four quick drops, exactly even. In the space after them I heard Nell take a breath to join me for the ending.

Four twenty-seven.

“I still like the original,” I said.

“I like you playing it,” said Nell. “You've got the high bit much cleaner than me. I like this one better, though.”

Mr. Vale was at his desk unwrapping his sandwich. He had a slice of tomato balanced on one thumb. Clearly we were on our own.

“Passing,” said Priya.

“Passing,” said Gus.

They waited. I wanted that long opening note with the whole auditorium quiet around it. I'd already pictured my brother recognizing the tune from the hallway and whispering to Mum.

“Passing,” I said finally. “But let me play the opening on my own sometime. At the summer assembly or something.”

“Ask him now,” said Nell.

Mr. Vale put the tomato back in his sandwich. “Come see me Monday. Bring the music.”

Then the choir came in, thirty people all going *mee may mah moh moo* at different speeds, and our twenty minutes were up.

During the break we ate rolls on the steps outside the auditorium. Nell had a foil packet of almonds from the plane. She picked out the whole ones and gave me the bits, which sounds mean unless you know I like the salt at the bottom.

“Were you hoping I'd miss the concert?” she asked.

I considered lying. “I was hoping you'd turn up about halfway through.”

“That's very specific.”

“I didn't want you stranded in Portugal. I wanted four minutes on clarinet.”

She shook some more almond bits into my palm. Through the doors we could hear the junior choir singing something about a blackbird. My brother appeared in his good shirt with the bottom button in the wrong hole.

“Are you doing the coat song?” he asked.

“Fourth time you hear it, that's me.”

He held up four fingers. Mum called him back before he could ask why.

When we walked onstage, the lights turned the audience into a few pale faces floating above a dark sea of jumpers. I could see my brother because he was still holding his hand up and Mum was trying to get him to put it down.

We tuned. In rehearsal I'd always listened for the moment my note lined up with Nell's and the little wobble between us disappeared. This time I could hear Gus turning a peg in tiny creaks. Priya rested her bow against the string. The cello began to rock.

Nell's opening note filled the hall. On the four quick ones she did that familiar tumble. Underneath her, my second part fitted so easily I could look up from the stand. Gus had tucked his left foot behind his right. His bow was poised halfway along the string.

My three notes came. I made the first small, the next a little bigger. On the third, Gus's elbow rose and the sound changed color right in front of me. From the seats it might have sounded like one instrument doing an impossible thing.

In the back row somebody dropped a program. Six weeks ago that would have been the only thing I'd heard. Now I was watching the last inch of Gus's bow. So was Priya. She caught his note and carried it up the cello string, and I heard, for the first time, what Nell was doing under her. Two short notes. *Chik chik.* Nell, who usually got the tune, was being Gus.

I nearly smiled myself off my reed.

Priya reached the top of her climb. Usually this was where, even while other people played, I started singing my own part inside my head. There wasn't room this time. I wanted to hear how long she'd stay up there.

She let the note hang for one lovely, dangerous instant. Then her bow eased and I took my breath with it.

My long note felt different coming out of hers. I let the first quick note stretch a hair. The next three went tumbling after it, just as Nell had played them at the start. Beside me I heard her second clarinet line rise to meet mine. We went up the last stairs together.

After the applause, as we bent to pick up our music, I saw my brother in the second row. He'd folded his striped daffodil program into a narrow tube. He put it to his mouth like a clarinet and wiggled his fingers at me.

Out in the corridor he played me what he'd heard. I expected the coat song. Instead he sang my three repeated notes into the end of the paper tube, each a little louder than the last.

Then he pointed it at me. He was waiting for the viola.

d8f25b9f911d0669.text:
# The Note Underneath

Mara’s clarinet case was on the chair I’d been looking at for six weeks.

I knew where she’d been. Her family had gone to visit her grandmother, and their flight home was supposed to land after the spring concert. I also knew the chair was exactly the same as mine, right down to the wad of gum stuck underneath. Still, all the way to school that morning I’d been picturing myself sitting in it.

“We got in last night,” Mara said. “I slept in my jeans.”

She looked it. There was a crease down one side of her face, and she’d put her reed on crooked. While she fixed it, I set my music on the stand. The second clarinet part landed on top. Its corners had gone soft from six weeks of being carried home inside my maths book. Underneath was the first part Ms. Vale had given me on Monday.

“Were you going to play first?” Mara asked.

“I was going to try it today.”

“Oh,” she said. She took the reed off again and turned it over.

Ms. Vale came in carrying the kitchen timer she used for sectional rehearsals. Behind her were Tessa with her flute and Dev with his cello, which he had to carry sideways to get past the doorstop.

“We’ve got twenty minutes before the choir needs the room,” Ms. Vale said. “By the time we leave, I need to know which version of ‘The Footbridge’ to put on your stands tonight.”

She held up two scores. The blue one was the original, with Mara on first and me on second. In that version the first clarinet carried a long tune over the cello’s plucked notes. My part was mostly on the offbeats, with four measures near the end where I got to come out from under everything.

The green score was the version Ms. Vale had made for three players when she thought Mara would be away. The cello bowed a short, repeating figure, and the first clarinet and flute tossed pieces of the tune back and forth. I’d been given the first clarinet part because I was the only clarinetist we expected to have. Ms. Vale had kept a second clarinet line in small print, marked *optional*. Mara bent over the green page to see what she’d be playing.

“I double Dev here?” she asked.

“An octave up, and only where you have notes,” Ms. Vale said. “See how much you can hear of his bow while you’re playing.”

She set the timer. It began to tick much louder than a thing that small should have been able to tick.

We played the green version first.

I’d practiced my opening four measures in my room until I could play them facing the wardrobe with the music behind me. At school, with Dev bowing underneath, the notes wanted to go a little faster than I’d practiced them. I went with him. By the time Tessa took over, we’d found a speed that made me feel as though I could get on a bike and take both feet off the ground.

Then I came in a beat early.

Tessa lowered her flute. “You cut off my bit.”

“I thought you were done.”

“I have one more note. The tiny one.”

It was a full-sized note. She meant it was short. We started two measures back, and this time I waited to hear it. Tessa flicked it up at the end of her phrase, and my answer came out so naturally I almost laughed into the mouthpiece. At the repeat, Dev dug into the low string and Mara came in above him. I could hear the bow catch before her note sounded. The two sounds together gave the whole thing a shove.

When we finished, Dev kept his bow in the air.

“That one’s fun,” he said.

I looked over at Mara. She was penciling a breath into her part.

We had eleven minutes left.

For the blue version, Dev put his bow across his knees. He plucked the first note, and Mara came in above it. Her first high note wavered as she got there. I knew the tune well enough to hear what she was aiming for. I’d played it on Monday night until my downstairs neighbor knocked on the radiator.

I came in on the offbeat and played too loudly. Mara’s next note disappeared somewhere inside mine.

Ms. Vale tapped my stand. “A shade less, Ivo. Let her finish the shape.”

I dropped so low on the next entrance that my reed gave a faint, horrible squeak. Dev’s mouth twitched. I spent the next eight measures looking hard at the music.

We made it to the place near the end where Mara’s line stopped and mine continued. At home I always took a fresh breath there, even when I meant to play the whole phrase through. There was nobody in my room to leave hanging in the silence.

This time Mara’s last note was still in the air when I reached mine. It was the same note, in a lower octave. I had enough breath. I kept going. For four measures the tune went exactly where it had always gone, and I heard, for the first time, how far down it traveled before Tessa came in. She entered so gently I could feel her note in the sound of mine before I could pick it out.

We finished. Someone from the choir tried the door and let it swing shut again.

“Five minutes,” Ms. Vale said. “Play those last eight bars both ways.”

In green, Tessa had the ending, with little jabs from my clarinet between her notes. We got them exactly together on the second try. I could imagine the front row sitting up at that sound. In blue, I lost the thread as soon as Mara stopped. I’d been waiting so hard for the moment I’d liked the first time that I missed the breath she took before it.

“Again?” I asked.

Mara nodded. This time I watched the edge of her sleeve rise. When she let her note go, I was there.

Ms. Vale turned the timer over. “What are we playing?”

Dev voted green. He liked using the bow. Tessa voted blue. She said she could hear everybody at the end. Mara ran one finger down the optional part, where there was a whole stretch of empty measures.

“Blue,” she said. “I like having somebody to hand it to.”

It bothered me that I knew exactly what she meant. I still wanted to play the opening of the green version in front of people. I wanted to get Tessa’s little note right with an audience there.

“Blue,” I said. “Can we start a bit slower than we did just now?”

Dev plucked the opening twice, leaving more space the second time. I nodded. It was the last sound we made before the timer went off.

We had forty minutes before the concert. In the canteen, I ate half a cheese sandwich and reread the green part. I got as far as the place where I’d come in early. Tessa had drawn a small arrow on my page pointing to the beat where her note would be. I rubbed a crumb off it with my thumb.

Mara sat down across from me and put her hands flat on the table.

“Are your fingers cold?” she asked.

They weren’t. Hers were. She’d washed them in the bathroom, where the hot tap only worked if you held it down with your elbow. I slid my paper cup of tea over to her. She wrapped her hands around it.

“I heard you from the corridor before I came in,” she said. “You were playing the beginning.”

“Did you hear me miss the high note?”

“I thought that was the door.”

I laughed. Then I folded the green part once and put it in my case. I could still have played the opening from memory. I tried the fingerings under the table until Ms. Vale came to get us.

Onstage, the lights made it hard to see past the second row. I’d spent the break imagining exactly where my dad would be sitting. Now all I could find was one of his shoes sticking into the aisle. He always crossed his ankle over his knee at the movies, too.

Dev put his thumb against the string. From my chair I could see the small dent it made in the pad of his thumb before he let go. I watched for the next one. The slower pace gave each plucked note time to get all the way out into the hall before mine came in.

Mara reached the high note cleanly. A little farther on, she took a breath in a place she hadn’t in rehearsal. I heard the gap and almost pushed my next note into it. Then Tessa’s flute came through from the other side of the stand. There had been room for her there all along. I eased back enough to hear where she ended.

Near the last page turn someone in the audience coughed twice. I looked up anyway. Mara’s sleeve rose. On the green page I’d spent the break reading, I would have had two quick notes right there, with Dev’s bow under me. Here he plucked once and lifted his hand. I could hear the faint sound of Mara’s keys as she came down to the note she would leave me.

For those four bars I could see my dad’s shoe, the pale edge of Tessa’s music, and the place where my own thumb had worn the corner of the page smooth. I’d been playing the phrase to my wardrobe for weeks, always speeding up a little at the end because there was nothing after it in my room. This time I let the last note take its full length. Tessa came in while I still had air, and for the last beat I could hear her better than I could hear myself.

We held still. In the dark beyond the second row somebody drew a breath. Then came the clapping, and Dev had to nudge my shoe with his before I remembered to stand.
